topic: My Salt Glands Can Excrete Enough Salt to Match Drinking Seawater Every Day
title: My Tongue Filters Seawater. Your Kidneys Can't.
description: Your kidneys tap out at 1200 mOsm. My tongue secretes salt at twice the ocean's concentration. Professor Croc breaks down 26 lingual glands, Na+/K+-ATPase pumps, and how to dump 35g of salt a day without losing water.
staircase: Seawater packs 35 grams of dissolved NaCl per liter creating 1000 mOsm per liter of osmotic pressure, triple your blood plasma at 300 mOsm per liter.
That 700 mOsm gradient pulls water out of your cells by osmosis through aquaporins, so drinking seawater dehydrates you.
Mammal kidneys max out at 1200 mOsm per liter urine via countercurrent multiplication in the Loop of Henle, so dumping 1000 mOsm seawater still costs you half a liter of fresh water.
Marine reptiles bypass that limit with a hidden ability: 20 to 26 extrarenal lingual glands that excrete salt without losing water.
Those glands use Na+/K+-ATPase pumps on the basolateral membrane to actively pull sodium from blood at 100.8 micromoles per 100 grams body mass per hour when saltwater-acclimated.
Inside secretory tubules they concentrate that sodium chloride to 600 to 1200 milliequivalents per liter, roughly twice seawater's salinity.
Blood flow to the tongue spikes via VIP signaling to deliver more salt, tripling secretion from 31.6 micromoles in freshwater to 100.8 micromoles in saltwater.
The hyper-concentrated brine at 2000 mOsm per liter drips onto the tongue surface and is sneezed or washed away, removing salt while conserving water.
Because salt leaves without water, the 35 grams you drank stays outside while the liter of water you drank stays inside you.
Over 24 hours that loop in its final form can dump enough salt to balance drinking about one liter of seawater per day, achieving full seawater tolerance.
